title: How to resize a design in Canva on Mac: step by step with custom sizes
metaTitle: How to Resize a Design in Canva on Mac, Step by Step
description: How to resize a design in Canva on Mac: pick a preset or custom size, choose the pages, then check each one before you export.
targetKeyword: how to resize a design in canva on mac
intro: To resize a design in Canva on Mac, open the design, click Resize in the top toolbar, and pick a preset or enter your own width and height. Then choose all pages or specific pages, and pick whether Canva copies the design or changes it in place.
tldr: Open the design, then click Resize in the top toolbar of the Canva editor.
Pick a preset size, or choose Custom size, enter a width and height, and lock the aspect ratio if you want the same proportions.
Choose all pages or specific pages before you confirm.
Pick Copy and resize to keep the original, or resize this design to change the current file in place.
Check every page and every element before you export, because resizing moves things.

blocks.text: Before you resize: what changes and what stays
Resizing looks like one click, but the layout underneath changes too. Text can wrap onto a new line. Photos can crop. Shapes and lines can shift when the proportions change.

Decide what you need before you start. A new version keeps your original for later. A change in place is quicker, but the old layout is gone unless you saved a copy first. If the design is client work or a template you reuse, duplicate it before you resize. The steps are in [how to duplicate a design in Canva on Mac](/how-to/duplicate-a-design-in-canva).

Pick the target size before you open the dialog. Social posts, flyers, and presentation slides each need different dimensions. Choose the size you need, then review the layout. Do not start from whatever size happens to be open.
Prepare the design before you resize

A tidy design resizes better. Delete hidden or empty elements first, because they still move with the layout and make the check slower. Keep headlines and body copy in text boxes, so you can widen them when the layout changes.

Check your photos too. Resizing keeps the detail in an image the same, so a blurry source stays blurry in a bigger frame. Replace weak images before you resize, not after. Make a short list of the pages you will change, so you pick the right pages in the dialog.
Step by step: resize a design in Canva on Mac

The steps below follow the Resize flow that third-party tutorials describe for the Canva editor on macOS. Canva's own Help Center pages could not be checked while this page was written. Confirm each label on your screen before you click, because labels can differ by app version and plan.
Most of the time goes to checking the result, not to the clicks, so leave room for that. The steps themselves are short.
Resize one page or every page

The page choice decides how much work Canva does. A single-page design has no decision to make. A multi-page design, such as a carousel, a slide deck, or a menu, asks whether to apply the resize to all pages or to specific pages.
Choose all pages when the whole set needs the same format. A carousel for a social feed is a good example. Every slide should share one shape, so you apply the new size to all of them at once.

Choose specific pages when only some of them need the new size. A cover page may need a different shape while the inside pages stay as they are. Select only the pages that change, and leave the rest alone.

Here is a worked example. Say you have a deck of slides built in a square format. You need a wide version for a presentation screen. Select every slide and pick the wide size. Then review the middle slides first, because they often hold dense charts or long text.
Check the page count before you confirm. A selection that looks like all pages can miss a page at the end. Scroll to the last page and confirm it is in the set.
Copy and resize or resize this design: which one to pick

When you confirm the size, some versions of the dialog ask what should happen to the original. Copy and resize makes a new version and leaves your design alone. Resize this design changes the current file in place. Trupeer's guide says the result depends on the page selection, so read the dialog before you confirm.

blocks.caption: Resize options as described in third-party guides, not Canva's own help pages.

blocks.text: If you are unsure, pick Copy and resize. A copy adds one more file to tidy up later. A changed original can cost you the layout you spent time building.
Undo helps in the moment. A copy is easier to trust when you come back to the file days later, and it is easier to compare two layouts side by side.
Custom sizes, aspect ratio and the pixel limit

A custom size takes two numbers, width and height. The guides give them in pixels. Lock the aspect ratio when the new shape should keep the old proportions. Turn the lock off when you need a different shape, such as a tall format from a square post.

Here is how the lock changes the result. With the lock on, changing one value usually changes the other to match. The design keeps its proportions, and the layout scales as one piece. With the lock off, each value stands alone, so the design can stretch or squeeze.
Turning the lock off gives you any shape you like. The layout then needs more repair afterward, so budget time for it. Big changes in shape need the most work, so start from a copy.

Canva also has a maximum size. One third-party guide gives it as 8000 x 3125 pixels. Canva's own pages could not be checked to confirm that figure, so treat it as a planning number. If a value is rejected, try a smaller one.
Resizing changes the frame, not the detail inside a photo. A small, soft photo stays soft when you put it in a bigger frame. If you need a sharper print, start with a larger image file instead.
A worked example: one square post, two formats

Say you built a square post for a product launch. You now need a tall version for a story and a wide version for a website header. Start by duplicating the square post. Name the copy so you know which file is which.

Resize the copy to the tall format with the aspect ratio lock off, because the shape changes a lot. Move the headline and photo until they sit inside the new frame. Then check the logo, since it often ends up too close to an edge.
Next, make the wide version from the square original, not from the tall copy. Starting from the tall copy carries over the changes you already made. A fresh start keeps each format clean.
Review both versions on every page, then export each one. Keep the square original as your master, so you can repeat the job the next time you launch something.
Use the format option for another platform

Resize is not the only route. Canva also has a separate option that builds a new format from your current layout. CapCut's guide describes a one-click tool for other sizes and formats, with presets for Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, and Twitter.
Use this route when you want the same design in a second format, such as a feed post and a story. Check whether the original changes before you confirm.
Guides do not agree on the name, and it may have changed over time. Look for an icon near the Resize button, or a matching entry in the menu bar. Trust the label on your screen.
Kwebby's guide says this option is only for Pro users. That article is from October 2023, so check the plan rules before you rely on it.
What happens to photos, text and shapes

Text is usually the first casualty. A headline that fit on one line can wrap onto two, which pushes the rest of the layout down. Shorten the copy or reduce the font size before you fix the spacing. Widening the text box also helps.

Photos crop when the frame changes shape. Check that the subject still sits inside the frame, especially faces and product labels. Move the crop until the important part sits well. Shapes and lines can stretch or shift, so look at borders and dividers too.

Work in a fixed order. Fix text first, because its size drives everything below it. Then move photos, and finish with shapes and lines. This order stops you from fixing a photo that a headline is about to push out of place.
Which Canva plan you need for resizing

Plan rules are where the sources disagree most. Kwebby says the format option is available only to Pro users. Its article is dated October 2023 and was updated in July 2024, so the rule may have changed since.

Trupeer says Pro users can use Resize in the top toolbar, while free users must create a new design with custom dimensions. It also says free users cannot resize existing designs directly. Those two claims do not fit together, so do not rely on either one.
Check your own account. Open the Resize option and see what it offers you. Then check the plan details on Canva's pricing page before you buy or upgrade, because plan details change.
Mistakes people make when they resize a design

items: Resizing the only copy. Duplicate the design first, then resize the duplicate.
Skipping the check on the last page. Errors often sit at the end of a deck.
Turning off the aspect ratio lock by accident. Photos then stretch to fill the new shape.
Expecting a small photo to look sharp in a larger frame. The detail does not change.
Forgetting the text. Long headlines overflow, and small type becomes hard to read.
Resizing every page when only one page needs the new format.

blocks.text: Most of these mistakes come from rushing the dialog. Slow down at the page choice and at the lock setting. Those two settings cause much of the trouble.
Check the result before you export

Look at each page at full size, not in a thumbnail. Start with text, because wrapping and overflow are easy to miss at small size. Then check photos and shapes, and finish with the spacing near the edges.

Edges matter. Elements that sat near the old border can now sit too close to the edge of the page. For print, that can mean a trim risk. For social posts, the platform may crop the image. Move those elements inward before you export.
Budget time for this step. A long deck takes longer to check than to resize. Skipping the review is a common reason a resized design goes out with an error on it.
Do one more pass after you export. Open the exported file in Preview, which comes with every Mac, and scroll through it. Small problems show up better in a file than in the editor.
Fixes when a resize goes wrong

Most bad resizes come from a short list of causes: a size past the limit, a stretched photo, or a page nobody checked. Fix elements with the corner handles, or enter exact dimensions when the editor offers them.
If the result is worse than the original, go back to the duplicate you made. Start the resize again from the copy instead of patching the broken version.
If a value is rejected, check it against the maximum size in the Custom size section. Enter a smaller width or height and try again.
If the Resize option is missing, check that you are in the editor and not on the home page. Plan rules can also hide the option, so check your plan before you go further.
How sure this page is

This page is built from third-party tutorials and Canva's public Mac download page. The download page confirms that the Mac app runs on Intel and Apple chips. It does not show an app version, so the labels here may not match your screen.
Two of the tutorials are older. Kwebby's article is dated October 2023, and CapCut's guide is dated September 2025. Use them as a starting point, not a final word.
No keyboard shortcut for resizing was confirmed for this page, so none is listed. Check Canva's help for a shortcut list if you want one.
What to do next

Once the first resize works, repeat it for each format you need. Keep one master design and resize copies from it. That keeps your fonts and colors in one place. For more on the workflow, read [Canva for social media managers on Mac](/for/social-media-managers/canva).

If the app misbehaves during a resize, update or reinstall it before you rebuild anything. The install and update steps are in [how to download Canva desktop app on Mac](/how-to/download-and-install-canva-in-canva).
If you resize often, write a short checklist. Include the page choice, the lock setting, the copy choice, and the last-page check. A checklist catches the errors that people miss when they rush.

faq.question: Can I resize a design in Canva on Mac without keeping the original?
faq.answer: Yes. Choose the option that resizes the current design in place, if your version offers it. Duplicate the design first if you might need the old size later.

faq.question: Where is the Resize button on a Mac?
faq.answer: Look along the top toolbar of the editor for Resize. Some guides also mention a Resize entry in the File menu. Labels vary, so trust the label on your screen.

faq.question: What does the format option do?
faq.answer: CapCut's guide describes a one-click tool for other sizes and formats, with presets for social platforms, custom width and height, and a preview before export. Guides name it differently, so match the label on your screen.

faq.question: Why won't Canva accept my custom size?
faq.answer: The value may be past the maximum. One third-party guide gives 8000 x 3125 pixels as the limit. Enter a smaller width or height and try again.

faq.question: Does resizing a design lower its quality?
faq.answer: Resizing moves and scales the layout. A photo in a smaller frame gets cropped, and a small photo stays soft when you enlarge its frame.

faq.question: Can I resize only one page of a multi-page design?
faq.answer: Yes. In the resize dialog, choose specific pages instead of all pages, then confirm the selection before you continue.

faq.question: Do I need a Pro plan to resize a design?
faq.answer: The sources disagree. Check the plan details on Canva's pricing page before you rely on any one tutorial.

faq.question: Is there a keyboard shortcut for resizing in Canva on Mac?
faq.answer: No resize shortcut is confirmed for this page. Use the top toolbar, and check Canva's help for a shortcut list.

task: Resize a Canva design on Mac
appliesTo: Canva editor on macOS, desktop app or web editor
requirements: A Mac with the Canva desktop app, or a Canva account in a browser
The design open in the Canva editor
The width and height your target platform needs
A duplicate of the design if you want to keep the original

steps.name: Open the design
steps.text: Open Canva on your Mac and open the design you plan to resize. If you use the desktop app, you can also open the design from the Dock. Let it load fully before you continue, especially if it has many photos or pages.
steps.tip: Duplicate the design first if you may need the original later.

steps.name: Find Resize in the top toolbar
steps.text: Look along the top of the editor for Resize. Some guides show it with an icon, and some show a matching option in the same area. If you see neither, check the File menu in the Mac menu bar for a Resize entry.
steps.tip: Labels differ between guides. Trust the label on your screen over any article.

steps.name: Pick a preset or a custom size
steps.text: Choose one of Canva's predefined sizes for a common platform. For anything else, choose Custom size, then type a width and a height in pixels. Lock the aspect ratio if the new shape should keep the old proportions.

steps.name: Choose the format option for another platform
steps.text: If you need the design in another format, open the format option and pick a size from its presets. Click Continue when the dialog asks you to confirm. Canva then builds the new version from your layout.
steps.tip: This option builds a new format from your current layout. It is separate from Custom size.

steps.name: Choose all pages or specific pages
steps.text: Multi-page designs ask which pages to resize. Select all pages when the whole set needs the same format. Select specific pages when only a few need a new size.
steps.tip: Scroll to the last page to confirm it is in your selection.

steps.name: Choose copy or change in place
steps.text: If the dialog offers Copy and resize, Canva makes a new version and keeps the original. If it offers resize this design, Canva changes the current file. Pick the option that matches what you need to keep.
steps.tip: If you are unsure, choose Copy and resize. You can delete the copy later after you check it.

steps.name: Fix elements that moved
steps.text: Click an element and drag its corner handles to resize it, or enter exact dimensions if the editor shows them. Work through text first, then photos, then shapes and lines. This keeps the spacing sensible as you go.

steps.name: Check every page before you export
steps.text: Scroll through each page at full size. Look for wrapped text, cropped photos, and elements close to the edge. Fix them, then export the design the way you usually do.
steps.tip: Open the exported file in Preview for one last look.

troubleshooting.fix: Check that you are in the editor, not the home page. Plan rules may also hide the option, so check your plan on Canva's pricing page.

troubleshooting.problem: A custom size will not accept my number
troubleshooting.fix: The value may be past the maximum. One third-party guide gives 8000 x 3125 pixels as the limit. Enter smaller values and try again.

troubleshooting.problem: A photo is stretched or cropped badly
troubleshooting.fix: Go back to your duplicate if the change is not what you want. When you resize again, keep the aspect ratio locked, then move the crop until the subject sits well in the frame.
Shorten the text, reduce the font size, or widen the text box. Then check the page again at full size.

troubleshooting.problem: I resized my only copy and want the original back
troubleshooting.fix: If you have no duplicate, rebuild the layout from your source photos and text. Duplicate the design before your next resize.

troubleshooting.problem: The format option has a different name in my app
troubleshooting.fix: Labels change across versions, and guides do not agree on the name. Use the option that builds the new format, then check the result on every page.
